topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Boolean Logic
topics.keyIdea: AND needs every input 1, OR needs any 1, XOR needs them to differ, and De Morgan swaps AND/OR when you negate.
topics.pixel: The gate's rule is AND plus NOT. Keycard AND NOT alarm. Easy. Unless you're a door.

slides.heading: NOT, AND, OR
slides.body: • NOT flips a bit: NOT 1 = 0. • AND is 1 only if all inputs are 1. • OR is 1 if any input is 1.
slides.example: A = 1, B = 0  →  A AND B = 0,  A OR B = 1,  NOT A = 0

slides.heading: NAND, NOR, XOR
slides.body: • NAND = NOT(AND), NOR = NOT(OR). • XOR is 1 when the inputs are different. • NAND and NOR are universal gates: any circuit can be built from just one of them.
slides.example: A = 1, B = 1  →  NAND 0,  NOR 0,  XOR 0

slides.heading: De Morgan's laws
slides.body:
• NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
• NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)
• "Break the bar, change the sign."  A truth table with n inputs has 2ⁿ rows.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.unit: Unit 2 · NCERT Ch 5: Getting Started with Python
topics.title: Python Basics
topics.keyIdea: / always gives a float, // floors, % gives the remainder and ** binds tightest; identifiers can't start with a digit.
topics.pixel: Python divides with one slash. Two slashes if it's feeling strict.

slides.heading: Tokens
slides.body: The smallest units of a program: • keywords (if, for, True) • identifiers (names you choose) • literals (5, 'hi', 3.14) • operators (+, ==) • punctuators ( : , ( ) ) Identifiers: letters, digits and _ only, never starting with a digit, never a keyword.
slides.example:
speed_2 = 10    # valid
2speed = 10     # SyntaxError

slides.heading: Data types
slides.body: • Numbers: int 7, float 7.0, complex 2+3j • bool: True / False • Sequences: str 'abc', list [1, 2] (mutable), tuple (1, 2) (immutable) • Mapping: dict {'a': 1} • None. type(x) tells you which.
slides.example:
type(7 / 2)    ->  <class 'float'>
type('7')      ->  <class 'str'>

slides.heading: Operators
slides.body: • / divides into a float (7/2 = 3.5), // floors (7//2 = 3), % is the remainder (7%2 = 1), ** is power. • Relational == != < >, logical and / or / not, identity is, membership in. • Precedence: ** first, then * / // %, then + −.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.unit: Unit 2 · NCERT Ch 6: Flow of Control
topics.title: Flow of Control
topics.keyIdea: range(stop) never includes stop; only the first true branch of if/elif runs; break exits a loop, continue skips a round.
topics.pixel: The taxi's loop never changed its condition. That's why it's been driving since Tuesday.

slides.heading: Three kinds of flow
slides.body: • Sequential: one line after another. • Conditional: if / if-else / if-elif-else (only the first true branch runs). • Iterative: for and while loops. Python marks a block by its indentation.

slides.heading: Loops and range()
slides.body: • range(start, stop, step) stops before stop: range(5) → 0 1 2 3 4. • range(2, 10, 3) → 2 5 8. • while repeats while its condition is True, so something inside must change or it never ends.
slides.example:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i * i)      # 1 4 9 16 25

slides.heading: break, continue, nesting
slides.body: • break: leave the loop at once. • continue: skip the rest of this round. • In a nested loop the inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer one.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.unit: Unit 1 · NCERT Ch 2: Encoding Schemes & Number System
topics.title: Number Systems
topics.keyIdea: Each binary place doubles (1, 2, 4, 8...); group bits in 3s for octal and 4s for hexadecimal; ASCII 'A' = 65.
topics.pixel: Rooftop rule: wrong answers fall off the building. Binary rule: there are only 10 kinds of people.

slides.heading: Four number systems
slides.body: • Binary (base 2): 0, 1 • Octal (base 8): 0–7 • Decimal (base 10) • Hexadecimal (base 16): 0–9 and A–F (A = 10 … F = 15) Each place is worth 'base' times the place to its right.

slides.heading: Converting
slides.body: • Decimal → binary: divide by 2 again and again, read the remainders bottom-up. • Binary → octal: group 3 bits from the right. Binary → hex: group 4 bits.

slides.heading: Encoding text
slides.body: • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters ('A' = 65, 'a' = 97). • ISCII: 8-bit code for Indian scripts. • Unicode: every script and emoji. UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per character, UTF-32 always 4.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.unit: Unit 2 · NCERT Ch 8–9: Strings and Lists
topics.title: Strings & Lists
topics.keyIdea: Indexes start at 0, negative ones count from the end, slices stop before 'stop'; strings can't be changed, lists can.
topics.pixel: Everything in The Source is a list. Even its feelings. Especially its feelings.

slides.heading: Strings: index and slice
slides.body: s = 'NEXUS': s[0] = 'N', s[-1] = 'S'. • A slice s[start:stop] stops before stop: s[1:4] = 'EXU'. • Strings are immutable: s[0] = 'X' is an error.
slides.example:
s = 'GLITCHED'
print(s[2:5], s[-2:], len(s))   # ITC ED 8

slides.heading: String methods
slides.body: upper(), lower(), title(), count('x'), find('x') (−1 if it's not there), replace(a, b), strip() (trims spaces), split() (makes a list of words), join().

slides.heading: Lists
slides.body: Lists are mutable: L = [3, 1, 2] • append(x) adds ONE item at the end, extend([…]) adds many, insert(i, x) • remove(x) deletes the first match, pop() removes and returns the last • sort() sorts in place, sorted(L) returns a new list.
slides.example:
L = [3, 1, 2]
L.append(5); L.sort()
print(L)          # [1, 2, 3, 5]

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Laws of Motion
topics.keyIdea: Net force changes momentum (F = ma); action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies; with no external force, momentum is conserved.
topics.pixel: Baron Von Friction hates this chapter. Read it twice. Out loud. Near him.

slides.heading: First law: inertia
slides.body: A body stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net external force acts on it. Inertia is the resistance to that change: more mass, more inertia.
slides.example: Bus brakes suddenly → passengers lurch forward

slides.heading: Second law: F = dp/dt = ma
slides.body: • Momentum p = mv. Force = rate of change of momentum; for constant mass F = ma. • Impulse = F × Δt = change in momentum. 1 N = 1 kg m/s2.
slides.example: 5 kg cart, net force 20 N  →  a = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s<sup>2</sup>

slides.heading: Third law, momentum, friction
slides.body: • Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, on a different body. • No external force → total momentum is conserved (recoil, rockets). • Friction: static ≤ μₛN, kinetic f = μₖN, and usually μₖ < μₛ. A circle needs a centripetal force mv2/r.
slides.example: Gun recoil:  m<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> = −m<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Kinematics
topics.keyIdea: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at<sup>2</sup>, v<sup>2</sup> = u<sup>2</sup> + 2as; for a projectile R = u<sup>2</sup> sin2θ / g, which is largest at 45°.
topics.pixel: In this game gravity is 34 m/s². In Physics Valley it's whatever the Lord says. In the exam, use 10.

slides.heading: Equations of motion
slides.body: For constant acceleration: • v = u + at • s = ut + ½at2 • v2 = u2 + 2as Slope of a velocity–time graph = acceleration; area under it = displacement.
slides.example: From rest, a = 2 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 5 s  →  v = 10 m/s,  s = 25 m

slides.heading: Projectiles: split the velocity
slides.body: • uₓ = u cos θ, u_y = u sin θ. • Horizontally: no force, so constant speed. • Vertically: accelerates at g downwards; at the top v_y = 0.

slides.heading: Range, height, time
slides.body: • Time of flight T = 2u sin θ / g • Max height H = u2 sin2θ / 2g • Range R = u2 sin 2θ / g: greatest at 45°; 30° and 60° give the same range. • Mass appears nowhere!

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Work, Energy and Power
topics.keyIdea: W = Fd cos θ, KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>, PE = mgh; the net work done equals the change in KE; power is work per second.
topics.pixel: Baron Von Friction is up ahead. Friction does NEGATIVE work. Be more positive than him.

slides.heading: Work
slides.body: • W = F d cos θ (joules). • Zero work when the force is perpendicular to the motion. • Negative work when the force opposes the motion (friction).
slides.example: Push 10 N through 3 m along the force  →  W = 30 J

slides.heading: Energy
slides.body: • KE = ½mv2 • PE (gravity) = mgh • spring PE = ½kx2 • Work–energy theorem: net work = change in KE. • With only conservative forces (gravity, springs), mechanical energy is conserved.
slides.example: Dropped from h:  v = √(2gh)

slides.heading: Power and collisions
slides.body: • Power = work / time = F × v (watt; 1 hp = 746 W). • Elastic collision: KE conserved. Inelastic: some KE lost. • Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions.
slides.example: Lift 50 kg by 2 m in 4 s  →  P = 50 × 10 × 2 / 4 = 250 W

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Oscillations
topics.keyIdea: A pendulum's period T = 2π√(L/g), a spring's T = 2π√(m/k); in SHM you're fastest in the middle and stop at the ends.
topics.pixel: Those bars ahead are pendulums. Lean WITH the swing to pump it higher. Physics, but make it parkour.

slides.heading: Periodic motion and SHM
slides.body: Motion that repeats is periodic. In simple harmonic motion the restoring force is proportional to the displacement and points to the centre: F = −kx. x = A cos(ωt + φ), T = 2π/ω, frequency ν = 1/T.
slides.example: ν = 2 Hz  →  T = 0.5 s

slides.heading: The simple pendulum
slides.body: For small swings T = 2π√(L/g). It depends on the length and on g, not on the bob's mass (and not on a small amplitude). 4 × the length → 2 × the period.
slides.example: L ≈ 1 m  →  T ≈ 2 s  (a 'seconds pendulum')

slides.heading: Springs and energy
slides.body: • Mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k). • Speed is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes; acceleration is greatest at the extremes. • Energy swaps between KE and PE; the total stays ½kA2.
slides.example: x = 0: all KE        x = ±A: all PE

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Gravitation
topics.keyIdea: F = Gm<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r<sup>2</sup> (inverse square); g ≈ 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> falls with height and depth; escape speed 11.2 km/s = √2 × orbital speed.
topics.pixel: The Source keeps deleting gravity. It's a law. Laws can't be deleted. I checked.

slides.heading: The universal law
slides.body: F = G m1m2 / r2, with G = 6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg-2. Double the distance → the force becomes ¼. Earth pulls you, and you pull Earth with the same force.
slides.example: r → 2r   ⇒   F → F / 4

slides.heading: g, height and depth
slides.body: g = GM/R2 ≈ 9.8 m/s2 at the surface. g decreases with height and with depth; at Earth's centre g = 0. Weight (mg) changes from place to place, mass doesn't.
slides.example: Moon: g ≈ g/6  →  a 60 kg person weighs about 100 N there

slides.heading: Orbits and escape
slides.body: • Orbital speed near Earth v0 = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s. • Escape speed vₑ = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s = √2 × v0. • Geostationary satellites: period 24 h, about 36 000 km up. • Kepler: orbits are ellipses, and T2 ∝ r3.
slides.example: vₑ = √2 · v<sub>0</sub>

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.unit: Unit 1 · Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
topics.title: Mole Concept
topics.keyIdea: moles = mass ÷ molar mass; 1 mole = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles; 1 mole of gas fills 22.4 L at STP.
topics.pixel: The door's fused shut. Make water. Two hydrogens, one oxygen, zero drama.

slides.heading: The mole
slides.body: 1 mole = 6.022 × 1023 particles (Avogadro's number). Molar mass = mass of 1 mole in grams: H2O 18, CO2 44, NaCl 58.5 g/mol. moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
slides.example: 36 g of water = 36 / 18 = 2 mol = 2 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> molecules

slides.heading: Gases and concentration
slides.body: At STP one mole of any ideal gas fills 22.4 L (22.7 L at the newer 1 bar standard). Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution.
slides.example: 4 g NaOH (40 g/mol) in 500 mL  →  0.1 mol / 0.5 L = 0.2 M

slides.heading: Laws and formulae
slides.body: • Conservation of mass; definite proportions (water is always 1 : 8 H : O by mass). • Empirical formula = simplest ratio (CH2O for glucose); molecular = n × empirical (C6H12O6). • The limiting reagent runs out first and decides how much product forms.
slides.example: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O :   4 g H<sub>2</sub> needs 32 g O<sub>2</sub>

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Structure of Atom
topics.keyIdea: Z = number of protons; a shell holds 2n<sup>2</sup> electrons; fill orbitals by Aufbau (n + l), at most 2 per orbital (Pauli), singly first (Hund).
topics.pixel: These element creatures used to be the periodic table. Know what's inside them and they calm down.

slides.heading: Inside the atom
slides.body: Electron (−1, tiny mass), proton (+1), neutron (0) in a tiny dense nucleus (Rutherford's gold foil). Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes: same Z, different A (12C, 14C). Isobars: same A, different Z.
slides.example: <sup>23</sup>Na: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons

slides.heading: Quantum numbers
slides.body: • n shell (energy) • l subshell: 0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d, 3 = f • mₗ orbital: −l … +l • mₛ spin: +½ or −½ A shell holds 2n2 electrons; orbitals per subshell: s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7.
slides.example: n = 3 can hold 2 × 3<sup>2</sup> = 18 electrons

slides.heading: Filling the orbitals
slides.body: • Aufbau: lowest energy first (n + l rule): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p … • Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers (max 2 per orbital). • Hund: fill equal-energy orbitals singly first.
slides.example: O (Z = 8): 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>4</sup>      Cr: [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>  (half-filled is extra stable)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.unit: Unit 4 · Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
topics.title: Chemical Bonding
topics.keyIdea: Ionic = electron transfer, covalent = sharing; in VSEPR lone pairs squeeze bond angles: CH<sub>4</sub> 109.5°, NH<sub>3</sub> 107°, H<sub>2</sub>O 104.5°.
topics.pixel: The Lord of the Lab taught the elements to refuse to bond. Show them how it's done.

slides.heading: Why atoms bond
slides.body: Atoms bond to reach a stable octet (a duet for hydrogen). • Ionic: electron transfer between a metal and a non-metal (Na+Cl-). • Covalent: electron sharing between non-metals: single, double or triple bonds.
slides.example: N≡N: a triple bond, very strong, very unreactive

slides.heading: VSEPR shapes
slides.body: Electron pairs repel and spread out; lone pairs repel more than bond pairs. BeCl2 linear 180° • BF3 trigonal planar 120° • CH4 tetrahedral 109.5° NH3 pyramidal 107° • H2O bent 104.5°
slides.example: H<sub>2</sub>O: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs  →  bent, 104.5°

slides.heading: Hybridisation, σ and π
slides.body: • sp → linear 180°, sp2 → trigonal planar 120°, sp3 → tetrahedral 109.5°. • σ bonds: head-on overlap; π bonds: sideways overlap. Double bond = 1σ + 1π, triple = 1σ + 2π. • Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to F, O or N) gives water its high boiling point.
slides.example: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>: each carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, the C=C is 1σ + 1π

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.unit: Unit 3 · Classification of Elements and Periodicity
topics.title: Periodic Trends
topics.keyIdea: Across a period → atoms get smaller, harder to ionise and more electronegative; down a group ↓ they get bigger and easier to ionise.
topics.pixel: Answer platforms ahead. Pick the trend, not the vibes. Wrong ones dissolve. Like sodium in water.

slides.heading: The modern periodic law
slides.body: Properties repeat with atomic number (Moseley), not atomic mass. 18 groups, 7 periods; s, p, d and f blocks. Group 1 alkali metals • group 17 halogens • group 18 noble gases • d-block transition metals.
slides.example: Li, Na, K: same group → similar chemistry

slides.heading: Across a period →
slides.body: • Atomic radius decreases (more protons pull on the same shell). • Ionisation enthalpy generally increases. • Electronegativity increases; metallic character decreases.
slides.example: Period 3: Na is the biggest atom, Cl the smallest

slides.heading: Down a group ↓
slides.body: • Atomic radius increases (a new shell each period). • Ionisation enthalpy decreases; electronegativity decreases. • Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all.
slides.example: Caesium loses its outer electron far more easily than lithium

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Redox Reactions
topics.keyIdea: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number up), reduction is gain (down); the oxidising agent is itself reduced.
topics.pixel: The Source is ALL oxidising agent. It takes electrons. And dignity.

slides.heading: Oxidation and reduction
slides.body: Oxidation = loss of electrons (oxidation number goes up). Reduction = gain of electrons (oxidation number goes down). OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. They always happen together.
slides.example: Zn + Cu<sup>2+</sup> → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + Cu :   Zn is oxidised, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced

slides.heading: Oxidation numbers
slides.body:
• A free element = 0.   • O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides).   • H is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides).
• They add up to 0 in a neutral compound, and to the charge in an ion.

slides.heading: Agents
slides.body: • The oxidising agent takes electrons, so it is itself reduced. • The reducing agent gives electrons, so it is itself oxidised. • Disproportionation: one element is both oxidised and reduced.
slides.example: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>   (O: −1 → −2 and 0)

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
topics.keyIdea: All cells come from cells; mitochondria make ATP, ribosomes make proteins, the Golgi packs and lysosomes digest.
topics.pixel: We're microscopic now. Everything around us is a cell. Including that thing waving at us. Don't wave back.

slides.heading: Cell theory
slides.body: Schleiden and Schwann: living things are made of cells. Virchow added 'Omnis cellula-e cellula': every cell comes from a cell. • Prokaryotes (bacteria): no nuclear membrane, no membrane-bound organelles, 70S ribosomes. • Eukaryotes: a true nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes.
slides.example: E. coli: prokaryote.  Your skin cell: eukaryote.

slides.heading: Organelles
slides.body: • Mitochondria: aerobic respiration, ATP (with their own DNA). • Chloroplasts: photosynthesis. • Ribosomes: protein synthesis (no membrane). • RER makes proteins, SER makes lipids. • Golgi: packs and secretes. • Lysosomes: digestive enzymes ('suicide bags').
slides.example: A cell that secretes lots of enzyme has lots of RER and Golgi

slides.heading: Membrane, wall, nucleus
slides.body: • Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): a lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it. • Plant cells add a cellulose cell wall and a large vacuole; centrioles are found in animal cells. • The nucleus holds chromatin; the nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
slides.example: Passive transport needs no energy; active transport uses ATP

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
topics.keyIdea: Air ends up in the alveoli; breathing in = the diaphragm contracts; O<sub>2</sub> rides haemoglobin, CO<sub>2</sub> travels mostly as bicarbonate.
topics.pixel: This is the airway. Everything here moves because of pressure. Like exams.

slides.heading: The airway
slides.body: Nostrils → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The epiglottis stops food going down the windpipe. Alveoli are thin, moist and wrapped in capillaries: O2 goes into the blood, CO2 comes out.
slides.example: Your lungs hold about 300 million alveoli

slides.heading: How breathing works
slides.body: Inspiration: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs → chest volume up, pressure down → air flows in. Expiration at rest is passive: the muscles relax.
slides.example: Lung pressure below atmospheric  →  air rushes in

slides.heading: Volumes and transport
slides.body: • Tidal volume ≈ 500 mL. Vital capacity = the most you can breathe out after a deepest breath in. • About 97% of O2 is carried by haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin). • CO2: about 70% as bicarbonate, 20–25% as carbaminohaemoglobin, about 7% dissolved.
slides.example: Gases move by simple diffusion, from high to low partial pressure

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Body Fluids and Circulation
topics.keyIdea: The SA node is the pacemaker; blood goes round twice (lungs, then body); arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back.
topics.pixel: Professor Plaque blocks arteries for fun. Know the route and he's just a speed bump.

slides.heading: Blood
slides.body: Plasma (about 55%) + formed elements: RBCs carry O2 with haemoglobin, WBCs defend, platelets clot. ABO groups depend on antigens on the RBCs: O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient.
slides.example: Clotting: thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin

slides.heading: The heart
slides.body: Four chambers: 2 atria + 2 ventricles. The SA node is the pacemaker; the AV node passes the signal on. Valves stop backflow: tricuspid (right), bicuspid/mitral (left), semilunar at the exits. Double circulation: pulmonary (heart ↔ lungs) + systemic (heart ↔ body).
slides.example: Body → RA → RV → lungs → LA → LV → body

slides.heading: Cardiac cycle and vessels
slides.body: • One cycle ≈ 0.8 s at 72 beats/min; stroke volume ≈ 70 mL → cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min. • 'Lub' = AV valves closing, 'dub' = semilunar valves closing. • ECG: P (atria), QRS (ventricles depolarise), T (ventricles recover).
slides.example: 72 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L of blood pumped every minute

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Neural Control
topics.keyIdea: Dendrite → cell body → axon; at rest the inside is negative (about −70 mV); Na<sup>+</sup> rushing in = depolarisation; the cerebellum keeps balance.
topics.pixel: We're sprinting down an axon. Jump node to node, just like the impulse does. Saltatory conduction, with extra screaming.

slides.heading: The neuron
slides.body: Dendrites receive, the cell body processes, the axon carries the impulse away to the terminals. A myelin sheath speeds conduction: the impulse jumps between the nodes of Ranvier.
slides.example: Myelinated fibres conduct far faster than non-myelinated ones

slides.heading: The nerve impulse
slides.body: At rest the outside is positive and the inside negative (about −70 mV), kept up by the Na+/K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in). A stimulus lets Na+ rush in → depolarisation (action potential); K+ flowing out → repolarisation.
slides.example: The impulse travels along the axon as a wave of depolarisation

slides.heading: Synapse and brain
slides.body: At a chemical synapse the impulse releases neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) across the synaptic cleft. Cerebrum: thinking, memory, senses • cerebellum: balance and coordination Medulla: breathing, heartbeat • hypothalamus: temperature, hunger, hormones.
slides.example: Every parkour landing you stick? Thank your cerebellum.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
topics.keyIdea: G<sub>1</sub> → S (DNA copies) → G<sub>2</sub> → M; mitosis keeps the chromosome number (2 identical cells), meiosis halves it (4 cells, with variation).
topics.pixel: The Source copies itself like a cell that skipped the checkpoint. Know the cycle, find the bug.

slides.heading: The cell cycle
slides.body: Interphase (about 95% of the time): G1 growth → S: DNA replicates → G2 preparation. Then M phase: karyokinesis (the nucleus divides) + cytokinesis (the cytoplasm divides). G0: a resting stage for cells that stop dividing (many heart and nerve cells).
slides.example: A human cell cycle takes about 24 h; M phase only about 1 h

slides.heading: Mitosis: equational division
slides.body: Prophase (chromosomes condense) → Metaphase (line up at the equator) → Anaphase (sister chromatids pulled apart) → Telophase (nuclei re-form). Result: 2 identical cells with the same chromosome number (2n → 2n): growth and repair.
slides.example: Onion root tip: the classic mitosis slide

slides.heading: Meiosis: reductional division
slides.body: Two divisions → 4 cells, chromosome number halved (2n → n): it makes gametes. Crossing over in prophase I (pachytene) shuffles genes → variation.
slides.example: Human: 46 chromosomes → gametes with 23
